Pathway enrichment across age: TB versus nonTB¶

Questions: How do TB and nonTB pathway levels vary with patient age, and does the difference between the groups change?

Age is continuous in the primary analysis. Smooth curves allow gradual, nonlinear changes without arbitrary age bins. The primary analysis fits each study separately. Section 6 adds an explicitly exploratory adult summary so the main figure can show just two curves, TB and nonTB, on one age axis. Study coverage appears directly below the curves. Children retain their own model; no curve connects the unsampled adolescent gap. Sections 4.3–4.4 and 6.3 add separate exploratory age-bin comparisons within studies and with studies combined.

How to read the results: Start with coverage in section 2. Section 4.1 adds age-specific TB–nonTB differences, confidence intervals and FDR-adjusted p-values; section 5 retains the continuous study-specific atlas. Section 6.3 shows six TB-relevant immune pathways, with two group curves, thin observed-age tracks and one compact pooled-test row. The explorer and linked detailed figures retain study-specific evidence. All 50 pathways remain tested and available. Section 7 retains robustness checks; section 8 distinguishes descriptive patterns from evidence.

These are cross-sectional age associations: different people sampled at different ages, not pathways followed as the same patients grow older. This is an exploratory analysis of the full eligible cohort, including participants previously used to train classifiers; it is not held-out model validation.

1. Settings and method¶

The main analysis uses the 50 human MSigDB Hallmark gene sets, a compact collection of biological programs. A patient's score measures how highly a program's genes rank within that patient's expression profile. We then model those scores against age, diagnosis and clinical covariates. This is single-sample pathway enrichment followed by regression, not over-representation of a thresholded list of differentially expressed genes.

Change settings here. Six TB-relevant immune pathways are selected for display using published human TB evidence, independently of their p-values in this dataset. This is a literature-led presentation choice made after the analysis, not a prospectively registered analysis subset. Every eligible pathway remains tested and shown in the atlas; all FDR families retain their original scope. Use the existing cfRNA TB overview kernel; dependencies are in the repository's requirements.txt.

Why these six pathways?¶

The focus set covers interferon responses, TNF signaling, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, inflammation and complement. The literature motivates these biological choices; it does not establish cfRNA pathway activation or age-dependent effects in this dataset. The mapping from a published mechanism to a Hallmark gene set is a presentation choice, particularly for TNF/NF-κB. Hypoxia, oxidative phosphorylation and other programs remain available in the complete analysis.

focus_rationale = '\n'.join(

    for row in TB_FOCUS.itertuples())
display(Markdown(focus_rationale))
  • Interferon-γ response: IFNγ-related transcription is part of the human active-TB whole-blood signature. Berry et al., Nature 2010
  • Interferon-α response: Type-I interferon-related transcription is part of the human active-TB whole-blood signature. Berry et al., Nature 2010
  • TNFα signaling via NF-κB: TB associated with TNF blockade supports the clinical relevance of TNF biology. Keane et al., NEJM 2001
  • IL-6 / JAK / STAT3 signaling: IL6/IL10 co-expression and constitutive STAT3 phosphorylation were observed in human TB patients. Harling et al., Cellular & Molecular Immunology 2019
  • Inflammatory response: Inflammatory and chemotaxis transcription accompanied human TB blood abnormalities and responses of reference monocytes to patient plasma. Ahor et al., Journal of Infection 2024
  • Complement: Complement-related blood transcription and rising circulating immune complexes accompanied early HIV-associated TB. Esmail et al., PNAS 2018

What the model tests¶

For each study and pathway:

pathway score ~ TB + smooth(age) + TB × smooth(age) + sex + HIV + country + count-read-length

The smooth is a natural cubic spline with 3 degrees of freedom by default. It is a regression curve that can bend gently; it is not an age bin or a rolling-window test. Constant covariates and exactly redundant nuisance columns are omitted, with an audit saved. Unknown HIV or sex is a separate recorded category; sensitivity analysis excludes these records.

  • Age-interaction test: jointly tests the TB × age terms. This answers whether the TB–nonTB difference varies with age. A small p-value for TB in one age range and a large p-value in another would not, by itself, answer that question.
  • Any-TB-difference test: jointly tests TB and its age interactions. This asks whether a TB–nonTB difference exists anywhere in the fitted study age range; it does not require the difference to vary with age.
  • Each question has its own Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) family covering all tested pathways × all studies. The primary question is the age interaction.
  • Intervals use heteroskedasticity-robust HC3 covariance and a t critical value. They are pointwise 95% confidence intervals, not simultaneous bands or FDR-adjusted evidence at each age.

Key assumptions and limits¶

Patients are independent after selecting one library per participant. Within a study, age is sufficiently smooth for a low-dimensional spline, and nuisance effects are additive. Adjustment does not establish causality or cell-intrinsic activation. cfRNA tissue/cell contributions, disease severity, clinical definitions, technical batches and unmeasured factors can still differ.

Display support requires both diagnoses within their observed age ranges and at least 10 participants of each diagnosis nearby (±2 years in PROTECT; ±7.5 years in adult studies). These windows only flag sparse estimates; they do not define fitting bins. Unsupported estimates are missing, never zero. The main fit and joint tests use the entire study age range, including sparse tails; section 7 repeats fitting after removing unsupported participants.

2. Which patients support an age comparison?¶

Read the complete local copied counts and audited metadata. Keep one representative library per participant, require QC pass, counts, a defined binary label and known age. The inherited selection prefers QC pass, available counts, the original historical library, then lexical sample ID; conflicting clinical annotations stop execution.

For PROTECT, TB means Confirmed TB and nonTB means Unlikely TB. Unconfirmed TB, healthy and latent comparison arms are excluded from the primary comparison; nonTB must not be read as healthy. Previous classifier training membership is retained here because this is exploratory biology, not classifier evaluation. Source files remain unchanged.

Coverage matters: PROTECT supplies the children; the other four studies supply adults. An apparent child–adult jump can therefore be a study, geography, assay or case-definition difference. The independent curves below cannot identify a biological transition across adolescence. The oldest observations remain visible in the coverage plot even when they cannot support a reliable TB–nonTB comparison.

3. Calculate each patient's pathway enrichment¶

  1. Read all 60,708 count rows and match exact gene IDs to the pinned GENCODE v38 annotation. Exclude PAR_Y duplicate representations and ambiguous symbols. No genes are chosen using TB differential expression or a trained model.
  2. Retain genes with ≥1 count per million in ≥10% of the complete analysis population. This creates one common, diagnosis-blind background for every patient. The pooled prevalence filter can miss programs detectable only in small subpopulations; this is a coverage limitation.
  3. Divide each gene count by its exon-union length, then rank genes within each patient (average tied ranks). A library-wide multiplier would not change these ranks. This approximates length-adjusted gene abundance; it is not isoform-aware TPM, and cfRNA fragment/GC/technical biases remain.
  4. For a set with m measured genes among N background genes, calculate the directional centered singscore:

[S = \frac{\text{mean gene rank}-(m+1)/2}{N-m}-0.5.]

The score ranges from −0.5 to +0.5; higher means the set's genes are ranked higher relative to other measured genes. Set members are treated as a unidirectional expression signature. A high absolute score is not itself a pathway p-value, enzyme activity or biological activation.

Require ≥15 measured genes and ≥20% coverage per set. Standardize each retained score by its mean/SD across all included people, using the same scale in every study. Plotted differences are in these pooled pathway-score SD units, not expression fold changes. Raw scores and scaling are also saved.

4. Fit continuous age curves within each study¶

All eligible pathway–study combinations are fitted. The joint age-interaction test is the primary evidence for age dynamics. The separate any-TB test should not be substituted for it. Clinical covariate distributions are standardized to the same study population for the two displayed group curves, so their difference is an adjusted comparison.

4.1 Evidence beyond a score in SD units¶

SD is a unit, not a significance test. At each reporting age, estimate the adjusted difference directly from the original study model:

[\Delta(a)=\widehat{\mathrm{score}}{\mathrm{TB}}(a)-\widehat{\mathrm{score}}{\mathrm{nonTB}}(a).]

Result What it tells us
Difference in pooled SD Size and direction: positive means higher in TB; negative means higher in nonTB.
Pointwise 95% confidence interval Uncertainty in that difference, calculated from the full HC3 covariance. It is not obtained by comparing the two groups' separate intervals.
age_contrast_q BH-adjusted p-value for a difference at a declared age. The full family includes all estimable pathways × studies × reporting ages. We flag q < 0.05.
age_interaction_q The original joint test of whether the TB–nonTB difference changes with age. This remains a separate question and test family.
Difference in original singscore units The same effect before SD scaling. This changes the units, not the p-value or amount of evidence. It is not an expression fold change or GSEA NES.

Reporting ages are declared in REPORT_AGES in section 1 (default: 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60), selected for this exploratory follow-up before calculating its age-specific p-values. They are not prospectively registered clinical cutoffs. Each study uses only supported reporting ages under the existing two-group coverage rule; unsupported rows retain their reason and counts, with no effect or p-value. The original 250 interaction tests remain unchanged. No interaction-significance screen is applied before these age-specific tests.

What counts as statistical enrichment here? A positive difference with age-contrast q < 0.05 supports a higher relative-expression pathway score in TB at that age within that study. A negative difference supports a higher score in nonTB. This does not demonstrate biochemical activation. BH adjustment targets the false discovery rate across discoveries under its assumptions; q is not the probability that an individual result is false.

The 95% intervals are pointwise and unadjusted for multiplicity. An interval can exclude zero while the FDR-adjusted test is not significant. Likewise, significant at one age and nonsignificant at another does not establish age dependence: use the joint interaction test. These results do not identify statistically significant continuous age windows or compare children directly with adults from different studies.

Methods: statsmodels linear contrasts, BH multiple-testing correction, singscore, and Gelman & Stern on comparing significance labels.

4.2 Effect direction and statistical evidence¶

The heatmap includes all pathways in alphabetical order. Color shows the adjusted difference; a black dot marks age-contrast q < 0.05. Only supported declared study–age combinations are shown. The complete table also retains all unavailable ages and their reasons. Adjacent columns are selected reporting ages, not age bins or significant age windows.

The following four study–pathway examples come from the TB focus set and are ranked by their smallest age-specific q-value. The left panels show both group levels; the right panels show their directly estimated difference. Open markers indicate no FDR discovery. This illustration selection does not change any test or FDR family.

4.3 Do TB and nonTB differ within the same age range?¶

This supplementary analysis groups patients into 0–<5, 5–<10, 10–<18, 18–<30, 30–<45, 45–<60 and 60+ years. The lower edge is included and the upper edge excluded; for example, someone aged exactly 30 enters 30–<45. These exploratory boundaries were declared before calculating the bin tests. They are editable in AGE_BIN_EDGES, but rerunning different cutoffs to obtain significance would add unaccounted selection.

Within each study and bin, fit a new model using only those patients:

pathway score ~ TB + linear age + sex + HIV + country + count-read-length

The TB coefficient compares the groups at the same age and recorded clinical characteristics under an assumed constant TB–nonTB difference within that bin. Keeping linear age in the model reduces remaining age imbalance inside broad bins. This is an age-range association, not proof of a difference at every exact age in that range. Models and their clinical reference populations differ from the continuous curves above; the curves are not refitted or recolored using these tests.

  • Require at least 10 TB and 10 nonTB patients, overlapping observed age ranges, at least 15 residual degrees of freedom and maximum leverage below 0.95. Perfect confounding of diagnosis with nuisance variables makes a bin unavailable. Redundant nuisance terms are audited; no unadjusted fallback is used.
  • Estimate the difference, pointwise 95% HC3/t interval and two-sided p-value. Apply one BH correction across all estimable pathways × studies × bins. bin_q < 0.05 is the discovery rule; this is a separate exploratory family from exact-age and interaction tests, not a correction across all analyses tried in this notebook.
  • Positive differences mean a higher pathway score in TB, negative differences a higher score in nonTB. A nonsignificant result does not prove equivalence. A discovery in one bin and none in another does not establish age dependence; the original interaction test still addresses that question.
  • Bins can change significance through sample size, model assumptions, age averaging and the number of tests. A new discovery would not establish that binning is the better model. No cutoffs are moved after seeing results. Broad bins may include ages with little or no local support; their result must not be read as a significant continuous age window.

The continuous models remain primary. See Altman & Royston on categorization, HC3 covariance, and Gelman & Stern on comparing significance labels.

4.4 Combine studies within each age bin¶

This final supplementary test combines all patients from all studies in the same declared age bin, while allowing each study its own baseline score:

pathway score ~ TB + linear age + study + sex + HIV + country + count-read-length

The TB coefficient estimates one common adjusted TB–nonTB difference in that bin. Study adjustment lets the studies have different baseline levels, so a study with generally higher scores is not automatically interpreted as a TB effect. Age and clinical/protocol covariates remain in the model. We assume the TB difference, linear age slope and nuisance slopes are shared across studies within each bin. More patients can improve precision under those assumptions; pooling does not guarantee greater power or make those assumptions true.

Use the same score scaling and bin boundaries as section 4.3. A pooled test requires at least two studies with both diagnoses and overlapping observed age ranges, at least 10 patients of each diagnosis in total, 15 residual degrees of freedom, maximum leverage below 0.95 and an identifiable adjusted TB coefficient. All patients in the bin enter a qualifying model, including patients from studies with only one diagnosis. A rare study or clinical category can let the model fit one patient exactly (leverage 1), preventing reliable HC3 uncertainty even with a larger total sample. No sparse or unusual category is dropped to force an acceptable test. Childhood bins contain only PROTECT, so they retain the existing study results and receive no duplicate pooled test.

Effects and pointwise 95% intervals use patient-level HC3 covariance and t inference. Pooled q-values use one separate BH family across every estimable pathway × bin. They do not adjust the combined search over every analysis in this notebook. HC3 is conditional on the model and observed studies; it does not estimate uncertainty from sampling new studies or unmeasured within-study dependence.

Check whether pooling is credible: a separate joint TB × study test asks whether the TB difference varies between studies within a bin; its q-values have their own diagnostic family. We also omit each contributing study and refit, retaining failures and effect shifts. A nonsignificant heterogeneity test does not establish equal effects. Omission checks are descriptive, not independent validation or alternative fits to choose from. The main fit is never replaced by the most favorable omission.

The Combined row in section 6.3 belongs to this pooled bin model. It does not test the continuous adult-summary curve above it, establish a difference at every age in a bin, or establish an age interaction. The original continuous and study-specific bin results remain unchanged.

Methods: Stewart et al. on participant-data models and study structure, HC3 covariance and BH correction. The study-adjusted model here is an observational adaptation, not a randomized-treatment causal analysis.

5. All-pathway age atlas¶

Color is the adjusted TB minus nonTB enrichment score: positive means higher in TB, negative means higher in nonTB. Every tested pathway is included. Rows are ordered by the smallest age-interaction q-value across studies, with p-value as a tie-breaker; row order is not evidence of significance. Each column uses that study's real age range. Grey cells are unsupported comparisons, not zero differences.

This heatmap displays estimates, not significant regions. Use the global age-interaction test table and the confidence intervals below for evidence. Hallmark sets overlap, so neighboring rows are not independent biological mechanisms.

6. Two group curves on one age axis¶

6.1 What the published examples suggest¶

The requested comparison is TB pathway levels versus nonTB pathway levels, including changes shared by both groups. A plot of only their difference would hide those shared changes. We therefore show two prominent group curves and move study inspection into an interactive selector, without splitting the main age axis into study rows.

Published source Relevant display or method Decision for this notebook
Bethlehem et al., Nature 2022, Fig. 1c and Fig. 3 Lifespan group curves summarize many studies after modelling study effects. Two group curves on one age axis; study details available separately. Their much broader age-overlapping data do not validate pooling our child and adult cohorts.
Lehallier et al., Nature Medicine 2019, Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 Smooth molecular trajectories, trajectory summaries and a separate sliding-window analysis. Continuous age can remain readable. Sliding windows ask a different question and depend on their width.
Javed et al., IEEE TVCG 2010 Controlled comparisons of multiple time-series displays show that performance depends on the comparison task and visual overlap. There is no universal winning chart. Reduce simultaneous curves and use interactive inspection for detail.
Altman & Royston, BMJ 2006 Categorizing continuous variables loses information and introduces arbitrary boundaries. Keep continuous age for fitting; do not change the analysis into hard bins solely to simplify the picture.
Riley et al., Statistics in Medicine 2020, section 4.4 Nonlinear covariate profiles require explicit synthesis assumptions and attention to within-study information. Declare the new adult model, keep study-specific levels, and check study sensitivity. This is an adaptation for observational TB data, not a reproduction of their treatment-effect meta-analysis.

Why keep the main curves continuous? Binning does not fix study–age confounding. A moving average of whichever studies happen to contribute at each age can bend simply because the study mixture changes. The adult summary instead fixes the study weights and clinical reference distribution at every predicted age. Sections 4.3 and 6.3 examine bins as a separate exploratory analysis, while retaining these original curves. No tuning parameter is selected for a more attractive or more significant result.

New exploratory summary model: retain the original PROTECT fit for children. For adults, allow study-specific baseline levels, study-specific TB level differences and study-specific clinical covariate effects, with a shared smooth age shape for each diagnosis. Predict both diagnoses at the same fixed adult study/clinical mixture. This shared-shape assumption is a modelling choice, not a consequence of the earlier study-specific results. The summary is not a pooled child-to-old-age biological trajectory, and child/adult score differences cannot isolate aging from study differences.

At ages covered by only some adult studies, the fixed-mixture curve relies on the shared-shape assumption to represent the others. Pooled local support does not mean every study has patients at that age.

The summary has its own age-interaction and any-TB FDR families (50 pathways × two populations), separate from the original 250 tests. The age-interaction test concerns the TB–nonTB gap, not whether either group changes with age. Study-shape diagnostics and leave-one-study-out fits assess the simplification; their limitations are reported below.

Read the two-curve timeline¶

Blue solid = TB; orange dashed = nonTB. Faint dots show observed patient scores; darker lines show adjusted group averages. The default curve-focused vertical scale retains every modeled 95% interval while clipping patient dots outside the displayed limits. Each figure reports the number outside the view. Switch the explorer to All patient scores, or open the full-distribution PDF, to see every dot. This changes only the display, not the fitted model or included patients.

Dots use actual ages and scores without jitter or covariate adjustment, so they need not center on the adjusted curves. The y-axis is the score in pooled SD units: 0 is the all-patient mean; +1 is one SD above it. Whiskers show pointwise 95% uncertainty. Adult intervals assume the shared age-shape model. The grey adolescent interval has no participants; other blank curve segments lack enough local support. Sparse-age patients remain in the data even where curves are withheld.

Thin tracks immediately below show observed ages by study. Adjacent occupied one-year intervals are merged into a single bar; every empty year remains a gap. These bars do not imply continuous sampling or sufficient statistical support. Counts are saved in study_age_coverage.tsv; intervals are lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive, except the final interval includes age 85. The tracks show both diagnoses together; counts are available in the explorer.

Use the interactive explorer to change the pathway, inspect a study in the same single plot, choose the vertical scale, or toggle dots/bands. The six TB focus pathways appear first; all 50 remain available. Coverage follows the selected studies. Individual-study views retain their own bin evidence; the combined view shows pooled tests. Open the statistics details for effects, intervals, q-values and unavailable reasons. Bin tests are separate from the continuous curves. Section 6.3 presents each focus pathway once in the compact layout.

    previous_index = pd.read_csv(index_path, sep='\t')
    assert previous_index.pathway.str.fullmatch(r'HALLMARK_[A-Z0-9_]+').all(), 'Unexpected previous figure name'
    previous_focus = previous_index.loc[previous_index.shown_in_notebook, 'pathway']
    for pathway in set(previous_focus) - set(focus):
        for prefix in ['timeline_', 'binned_timeline_']:
            for suffix in ['png', 'pdf']:
                (OUT / f"{prefix}{pathway.removeprefix('HALLMARK_').lower()}.{suffix}").unlink(missing_ok=True)

                                    'Subject': 'All eligible Hallmark pathways; one pathway per page'}) as pdf, \
     PdfPages(distribution_pdf, metadata={'Title': 'Full observed patient pathway-score distributions'}) as full_pdf:
    for page, pathway in enumerate(sorted(scores.columns), start=1):

                                          scores=scores, score_view=SCORE_VIEW)
        pdf.savefig(fig)
        timeline_index.append({'page': page, 'pathway': pathway,

        if pathway in focus:

        full_figure = plots.plot_summary_timeline(meta, summary_curves, pathway,

        full_pdf.savefig(full_figure)

6.2 Study-specific closeups and TB–nonTB differences¶

These closeups show the full confidence bands and make the childhood age range easier to inspect. The same diagnosis colors apply: blue = TB, orange = nonTB. Study identity is in the panel title.

These detailed figures are exported and linked below; set SHOW_STUDY_CLOSEUPS = True to embed them as well. They include three TB focus pathways in the largest childhood and adult studies, followed by difference curves for all six focus pathways. The horizontal zero line in a difference plot means equal adjusted scores. Shading is the pointwise 95% confidence interval. A changing-looking curve is a hypothesis until the joint age-interaction test supports it after FDR correction. PROTECT and ADTB are separate studies and their curves should not be joined across adolescence.

Do the other adult studies tell a similar story?¶

These independent study fits provide a consistency check. Different precision, supported age ranges and clinical composition can explain different-looking estimates. They are not longitudinal replication, and a pathway significant in only one study does not establish that the studies differ.

6.3 TB-relevant pathways: compact timelines¶

Each focus pathway appears once: two continuous curves, five thin observed-age tracks, and one Combined bin-test row on the same age axis. This main view removes the repeated study-test matrix, endpoint caps, vertical guides and duplicated text. The curves, intervals, patient dots and all statistical estimates are unchanged.

In the bin row, filled blue means higher TB scores at pooled q < 0.05; filled orange means higher nonTB scores. An open circle means no FDR discovery; × means the test is unavailable. A segment identifies the fitting bin, not a continuously significant age interval. The combined model adjusts for study and clinical covariates; it is separate from the continuous curves above.

The six choices are justified in section 1. All 50 pathways and all study-specific tests remain available in the linked PDFs and explorer. The detailed PDF restores the five individual-study test rows alongside the combined row. Their FDR families remain separate. The main view's childhood crosses mean no multi-study test because only PROTECT contributes, not an absence of children.

        & summary_tests.pathway.eq(pathway)].iloc[0]

        study_sensitivity=max(adult_test.loso_max_abs_TB_shift, adult_test.loso_max_abs_nonTB_shift))

7. Sensitivity to curve shape, missingness, batch and sparse ages¶

Repeat with 2 and 4 spline degrees of freedom; complete sex/HIV records; preparation-batch fixed effects; participants whose own age passes the primary local-support rule; and only count columns tagged 61×61. Scores and gene universe stay fixed, so these isolate model/population sensitivity. Batch adjustment excludes batches with fewer than 3 people to avoid singleton fixed effects. It still does not resolve all processing confounding. The original metadata reports processed reads as 61×61 throughout, but 31 ADTB count columns are tagged 150×150; the primary model adjusts the actual count-column tag, and the read-length sensitivity removes these 31 libraries.

Models with fewer than 15 residual degrees of freedom or maximum leverage ≥0.95 are explicitly skipped, not silently fitted. The primary results are never replaced by the variant with the smallest p-value. age_interaction_q corrects each variant across studies and pathways; age_q_across_sensitivities additionally corrects all successfully fitted sensitivity tests together. Sensitivity analyses are exploratory, not independent validation.

In [20]:
sensitivity_tables, sensitivity_diagnostics = [], {}
if RUN_SENSITIVITIES:
    own_age_support = pd.Series(False, index=meta.index)
    for study, group in meta.groupby('cohort'):
        width = PARAMETERS['child_half_width'] if study == 'PROTECT' else PARAMETERS['adult_half_width']
        own_age_support.loc[group.index] = analysis.support_mask(
            group, group.age_years.to_numpy(), width, PARAMETERS['minimum']).supported.to_numpy()
    variants = [
        ('spline_df2', 2, meta, False), ('spline_df4', 4, meta, False),
        ('complete_covariates', PARAMETERS['spline_df'], meta.loc[meta.sex.ne('Unknown') & meta.hiv.ne('Unknown')], False),
        ('prep_batch', PARAMETERS['spline_df'], meta.loc[meta.groupby(['cohort', 'prep_batch']).subject_id.transform('size').ge(3)], True),
        ('supported_ages_only', PARAMETERS['spline_df'], meta.loc[own_age_support], False),
        ('count_reads_61x61', PARAMETERS['spline_df'], meta.loc[meta.count_read_length.eq('61x61')], False),
    ]
    for name, df, subset, batch in variants:
        variant_parameters = {**fit_parameters, 'spline_df': df}
        table, _, info = analysis.fit_atlas(subset, scores, batch=batch, allow_skip=True, **variant_parameters)
        table['sensitivity'] = name
        sensitivity_tables.append(table)
        sensitivity_diagnostics[name] = {'participants': len(subset), 'excluded': len(meta) - len(subset), 'models': info}
    sensitivity_tests = pd.concat(sensitivity_tables, ignore_index=True)
    sensitivity_tests['age_q_across_sensitivities'] = analysis.bh_finite(sensitivity_tests.age_interaction_p)
    save_table(sensitivity_tests, 'sensitivity_tests')
    (OUT / 'sensitivity_diagnostics.json').write_text(json.dumps(sensitivity_diagnostics, indent=2))
    sensitivity_summary = sensitivity_tests.groupby('sensitivity').agg(
        tested_pairs=('pathway', 'size'), age_FDR05_within_variant=('age_interaction_q', lambda x: (x < .05).sum()),
        age_FDR05_all_variants=('age_q_across_sensitivities', lambda x: (x < .05).sum()),
        minimum_age_q=('age_interaction_q', 'min'))
    sensitivity_summary['participants'] = pd.Series({k: v['participants'] for k, v in sensitivity_diagnostics.items()})
    display(sensitivity_summary.round(4))
    save_table(sensitivity_summary, 'sensitivity_summary', index=True)
    for variant, info in sensitivity_diagnostics.items():
        for study, model_info in info['models'].items():
            if model_info.get('skipped'):
                print(f"Skipped {variant} / {study}: {model_info['reason']}")
else:
    display(Markdown('Sensitivity analyses were disabled in this run.'))

8. What can we conclude from this run?¶

This summary is calculated from the current executed results. A lack of FDR-significant interactions is not proof that pathways are age-invariant; it can reflect noise, sample size, sparse tails or model/measurement limitations.

The declared-age results in section 4.1, within-study bin results in section 4.3 and combined-study bin results in section 4.4 address different questions under different models and FDR families. Their effect sizes, confidence intervals and globally corrected q-values should be read together; the original interaction test remains the evidence for age dependence. No claim of a continuous statistically enriched age interval is made from pointwise curves or bin tests.

In [21]:

812 patients, 50 pathways, 5 independent study models. The primary analysis found 0 of 250 pathway–study interactions at FDR < 0.05 (smallest age-interaction q = 0.986). The separate any-TB-difference test identified 6 pathway–study associations at FDR < 0.05.

The data do not currently provide FDR-controlled evidence that the TB–nonTB enrichment difference changes with age under this model. The curves are exploratory estimates with uncertainty; visible bends should not be called established age dynamics.

The supplementary fixed-bin analysis found 7 of 550 tested study–pathway–bin comparisons at FDR < 0.05 (minimum q = 0.024). These are within-age-range associations under separate linear-age models. Their significance cannot be assigned to every exact age in the bin or used to claim an age-dependent TB difference. The original exact-age analysis and all continuous curves remain unchanged.

Combining studies within the same bins, with study and clinical adjustment, found 16 of 100 pooled comparisons at FDR < 0.05 (minimum q = 0.0013). The separate TB-by-study diagnostic identified 0 of 100 FDR-significant heterogeneity tests; that does not validate the common-effect assumption. Study-omission estimates and unavailable models remain visible. Pooling is exploratory and cannot create evidence from a single-study childhood bin or overcome an unstable adjusted fit.

No model identifies a continuous childhood-to-old-age trajectory. Children and adults were recruited in different studies, adolescence is unsampled, and sparse coverage and model stability limit the oldest-age comparisons. More age-overlapping cohorts and longitudinal sampling would distinguish age from study effects.

9. Reproducibility, outputs and references¶

Routine reruns use local copied data and pinned pathway/annotation resources; no download or classifier refitting is needed. The pathway regressions are refitted each run. The raw count matrix is deliberately recomputed once per run so there is no hidden stale score cache. The generated TSV files retain the complete test family, support flags, gene coverage, included participants, normalized scores, model diagnostics and sensitivity results. PDF and PNG figures are saved beside them in results/pathway_age/.

The shared-age views are saved as pathway_timelines_all.pdf (one page per eligible pathway, alphabetically ordered), pathway_timeline_index.tsv (page lookup), and timeline_*.png / .pdf for the focus pathways. The main timeline uses the exploratory fixed-composition adult model plus the original pediatric fit. Its separate summary tests, complete curves, diagnostics and leave-one-study-out curves are saved as summary_*. The interactive pathway_age_explorer.html also exposes the original individual-study curves. It embeds aggregate model estimates and rendered patient-dot images, without patient identifiers or machine-readable patient records. Original primary and sensitivity analyses are retained unchanged.

pathway_patient_distributions_all.pdf retains the full observed y-range, one pathway per page. age_contrasts.tsv contains every planned study/pathway/reporting-age combination, exact-age effects in SD and original score units, confidence intervals, p/q-values, local counts and unavailable reasons. age_contrast_diagnostics.json records the test family; age_contrast_summary.tsv and the heatmap summarize the complete family. age_contrast_examples.tsv records the four selected illustration pairs.

age_bins.tsv retains every planned study/pathway/bin combination, including unsupported fits, effects in both units, pointwise 95% intervals and the separate global bin FDR family. age_bin_counts.tsv, age_bin_summary.tsv and age_bin_diagnostics.json record counts, unavailable reasons, design checks and model assumptions. pathway_age_bins_all.pdf uses a compact pooled-test row; pathway_age_bins_by_study_all.pdf retains every individual-study test row. Both include all 50 pathways. pathway_age_tb_focus.pdf and binned_timeline_*.png / .pdf show the six literature-led immune focus pathways. tb_pathway_focus.tsv records their rationale, evidence scope, primary references and interpretation limits. This display selection does not change statistical test families.

study_age_coverage.tsv contains every study/year interval, including zero-count gaps, counts by diagnosis and the final inclusive boundary. pooled_age_bins.tsv contains all planned pathway/bin pooled contrasts and separate study-heterogeneity diagnostics. pooled_age_bin_summary.tsv summarizes the pooled family; pooled_age_bin_diagnostics.json records designs, assumptions, support checks and study composition. pooled_age_bin_leave_one_study_out.tsv retains every attempted omission, effect shifts and unavailable reasons; omission p-values are descriptive and never replace the primary pooled results.

The resource manifest records the full GTF and Hallmark hashes. reference/pathway_age/build_resources.py can rebuild the compact annotation from its recorded source files; ordinary reruns need only the saved compact resources. Old classifier inputs, normalization and results are separate from this analysis.

Method references:

  • Foroutan et al., single-sample scoring of molecular phenotypes: rank score and theoretical normalization.
  • singscore documentation: directional single-set scoring; the transparent Python implementation uses its published formula.
  • MSigDB Hallmark collection: definitions and acknowledgments; pinned local release 2026.1.Hs.
  • GENCODE human release 38: exact gene annotation and exon-union lengths.
  • Patsy spline regression: natural cubic spline basis.
  • statsmodels HC3 covariance: robust standard errors.

These scores quantify relative cfRNA expression programs. They do not prove pathway activation, cell-intrinsic regulation, causation or treatment response.
